comments.author: @RobertManning-l3s
comments.text: As an AirBnB/B&B owner, I concur that the tipping point is when prices exceed prevailing hotel costs.  In my case, I offer 2 or maximum of 3 rooms in a historic farmhouse with antique and historical displays.  I live in the remaining room and greet guests with a welcome basket.  The departure and arrival times are flexible (without additional costs), easy free parking, high end shampoos and soaps in bathroom, personal (new) TVs, and no extra cleaning costs unless left in an outrageous condition.  Plus, 69 private acres for games, metal detector hunts, hiking trails, and fresh coffee under grand Maple tree with a serenade of birds for breakfast.  I try hard to make the visit a unique experience and am available onsite to answer any questions or problems.  I even offer special sports and hunting packages.  If my guests are not satisfied and complain, I give a FULL DAY refund. Otherwise, why come to a "short-term rental" if is NOT a good price and offers a special experience!  AirBnB "hosts" need to exit the industry if the goal is to squeeze guest for more money.  And, I agree that there should be more stringent control over sale of houses for AirBnB rentals that contribute to the affordable housing crisis.  My approach is part of the solution and not the problem.

comments.author: @elenabogarin
comments.text:
I can agree that some Airbnb rules are ridiculous. But when people say, “I’d rather stay at a hotel because I don’t have to clean,” there’s a bigger picture being missed.

Most of the rules hosts have today exist because hosts have already been burned. These are people’s homes and investments not hotel rooms owned by huge corporations. We still have mortgages, electricity, water, maintenance, supplies, cleaners, and rising costs.

Guests have thrown parties, left vomit EVERYWHERE, left 10+ bags of trash, damaged things, ruined linens, and created hours of extra work. Some Airbnb cleaners charge $300–$500 for a normal turnover, and excessive mess can mean another cleaning charge on top of that.

I’ve absorbed those costs myself plenty of times, but eventually you can’t keep eating hundreds of dollars because a guest decided to leave the house trashed.

And yes, hotel housekeeping cleans up after you. But hotel housekeepers are employees. Many Airbnb cleaners are independent businesses that set their own rates and are not going to work for $100 to clean up someone’s disaster.

Not every guest is bad I’ve had amazing guests. But if you want to stay in someone’s home, basic respect for the home and the person cleaning it shouldn’t be controversial.

You don’t have to clean an Airbnb. But you also shouldn’t trash it because someone else is getting paid to clean.

comments.author: @wafiv
comments.text: Economist here: The downfall of AirBnB is when people thought they could run a business model that looked like a hotel versus a small mom and pop business that required them to be hands on. Hotels are able to hire maids who clean an entire floor of rooms (20-30) per day. Their per room cost once broken down is extremely cheap. That is not true for an AirBnB where you are paying a cleaning company likely and having to clean it everyday is honestly not economical. You have 2-3 rooms at most, with hotels having hundreds.
